Education only. Not for diagnosis, treatment or any clinical decision.

## In 60 seconds

Most AI-in-EP studies are retrospective. A 2026 meta-analysis found that machine-learning models
discriminated atrial fibrillation (AF) recurrence after ablation better than traditional risk scores,
pooled over 11 studies [@koh2026]; a 2025 EHRA, HRS and ESC statement found that no item of its
29-item AI reporting checklist was reported by more than 55% of the EP papers it reviewed
[@svennberg2025]. Moving up the evidence ladder means external validation, prospective use and,
for claims of patient benefit, randomized trials, of which EP now has examples
[@deisenhofer2025; @yao2021]. Reporting and appraisal tools exist for each stage
[@collins2024; @moons2025; @vasey2022; @cruzrivera2020; @liu2020]. Once deployed, a model meets new patients, devices and practice, so it
must be monitored, and changes to it follow a plan agreed in advance [@fdapccp2024]. This module
derives the sample size for a sensitivity study, the net benefit of a decision curve and the CUSUM
drift alarm, and the capstone lab takes an AI-ECG detector through validation, deployment, drift
and a controlled update.

## From the field

- **Discrimination is not enough.** In the meta-analysis of AF-recurrence models, pooled AUC was 0.80
  for machine-learning models against 0.58 for risk scores, with methodological quality assessed by
  PROBAST [@koh2026]. A multicentre model that added ablation quality metrics reported an internal
  AUC of 0.918 and AUCs of 0.992 and 0.951 in two external hospitals [@wang2026]: results to read
  with the appraisal questions of this module, not to adopt.
- **Reporting gaps in EP.** The EHRA AI checklist (29 items) was applied to 55 EP studies published
  between May 2021 and May 2024; trial registration, participant details, data handling and training
  performance were each reported by fewer than 20% [@svennberg2025]. LLMs have also been tested as
  reviewers against this checklist [@sluha2025].
- **Randomized evidence exists.** A cluster-randomized pragmatic trial of an AI-ECG tool in primary
  care increased new diagnoses of low ejection fraction from 1.6% to 2.1% [@yao2021]. In TAILORED-AF,
  a double-blind randomized trial, ablation guided by an AI algorithm in addition to pulmonary vein
  isolation met its primary endpoint of freedom from AF at 12 months, 88% against 70% with isolation
  alone [@deisenhofer2025]. A blinded randomized trial with Stanford and Cedars-Sinai authors found
  that cardiologists changed AI first reads of ejection fraction less often than sonographers' first
  reads (16.8% against 27.2% of studies substantially changed) [@he2023].
- **Regulators list what they have authorized.** The FDA keeps a public list of AI-enabled medical
  devices, notes that it is not a comprehensive resource, and states that it regulates devices,
  including AI-enabled ones, rather than AI as such [@fdaailist]. Researchers at Stanford analysed how
  the AI devices cleared by the FDA had been evaluated and made recommendations for their evaluation
  [@wu2021fda].
- **Validation across sites without moving data (NVIDIA).** A federated model trained with data from 20
  institutes predicted the oxygen needs of patients with COVID-19 with an average AUC above 0.92 and
  generalized better than models trained at a single site [@dayan2021]; NVIDIA FLARE is an open
  framework for such training [@roth2022nvflare].

## Derivations

### The evidence ladder

| Rung | Design | What it can show | Reporting or appraisal tool |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Development and internal validation | That a signal exists in these data | TRIPOD+AI [@collins2024]; PROBAST+AI [@moons2025] |
| 1 | External validation | That it transfers to other sites, devices, patients | TRIPOD+AI; PROBAST+AI |
| 2 | Prospective, non-randomized, often "silent" | That it works in the live workflow | DECIDE-AI [@vasey2022] |
| 3 | Randomized trial | That using it changes care or outcomes | SPIRIT-AI [@cruzrivera2020], CONSORT-AI [@liu2020] |
| — | EP-specific reporting | Items particular to EP studies | EHRA AI checklist [@svennberg2025] |

PROBAST+AI assesses model development (16 signalling questions) and model evaluation (18) across four
domains: participants and data sources, predictors, outcome and analysis [@moons2025]. DECIDE-AI covers
early clinical evaluation with 17 AI-specific and 10 generic items [@vasey2022]. SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI
extend the standard trial-protocol and trial-report guidelines to interventions with an AI component
[@cruzrivera2020; @liu2020].

**Key takeaways**

- Name the rung before reading the result; a retrospective AUC is not evidence of benefit.
- Use the matching checklist when writing and when reviewing.
- In EP, most studies are still on rungs 0 and 1 [@svennberg2025; @koh2026].

### How many patients?

To estimate a sensitivity near $Se$ with a 95% interval of half-width $d$, a study needs about
$z^2 Se(1-Se)/d^2$ patients **with** the condition. If a share $\pi$ of enrolled patients has it,
the total to enrol is [@buderer1996]

$$
n_{Se} = \frac{z^2\,Se\,(1-Se)}{d^2\,\pi}, \qquad n_{Sp} = \frac{z^2\,Sp\,(1-Sp)}{d^2\,(1-\pi)}
$$ {#eq-m45-n-sens}

and the study needs the larger of the two. At $Se = 0.9$, $d = 0.05$ and $\pi = 0.2$, that is 692
patients; at $\pi = 0.05$ it is four times as many. Lab part B checks the formula by simulating studies
and measuring the half-width of their Wilson intervals (m43).

::: {.demo #m45-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m45-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m45-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m45-d2-how-many-patients.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m45-n-sens with $z = 1.96$, the normal approximation to the binomial, independent
  patients and a known prevalence. The JavaScript is tested against `epml.evidence`.
- Slider values are illustrative, not targets from any guideline.
- What would change the result: several recordings per patient (the design effect of m35), a
  prevalence that differs from the one assumed, and sensitivities near 0 or 1, where the normal
  approximation is poor.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Sensitivity is estimated only on patients with the condition: rare conditions need large studies.
- Plan the sample size before the study, from the interval you need.

### Is the model useful? Decision curves

A model can discriminate well and still not help a decision. Decision-curve analysis [@vickers2006]
asks whether acting on the model beats acting on everyone or on no one. A threshold probability $p_t$
expresses how a clinician weighs a false positive against a missed case: at $p_t$ they are indifferent
between acting and not. For the rule "act if the model's probability is at least $p_t$",

$$
\mathrm{NB}(p_t) = \frac{\mathrm{TP}}{n} - \frac{\mathrm{FP}}{n}\cdot\frac{p_t}{1 - p_t}
$$ {#eq-m45-net-benefit}

Acting on no one gives 0; acting on everyone gives $\pi - (1-\pi)\,p_t/(1-p_t)$; a perfect model gives
$\pi$. A model is useful at the thresholds where its curve lies above both.

**Key takeaways**

- Net benefit puts true and false positives on one scale, weighted by the decision's threshold.
- Report the curve over the range of thresholds clinicians would use.

### Monitoring after deployment

A deployed model meets patients, devices and practice that differ from its validation data (m37's
dataset shift). Labels arrive late or never, but scores arrive daily. Page's cumulative sum
[@page1954] detects a lasting upward shift in a standardized daily statistic $x_t$:

$$
S_t = \max\bigl(0,\; S_{t-1} + x_t - \mu_0 - k\bigr), \quad S_0 = 0, \qquad \text{alarm when } S_t > h
$$ {#eq-m45-cusum}

The allowance $k$ ignores small deviations and the threshold $h$ sets how much evidence must
accumulate. Raising $h$ makes false alarms rarer and detection slower; for a large shift $\delta$ the
delay is close to $h/(\delta - k)$ observations. A score alarm says that something changed, not what;
finding out needs a labelled sample.

::: {.demo #m45-d1 badge="simulation"}
```{=html}
<div id="m45-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m45-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m45-d1-silent-drift.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: daily mean scores standardized to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 in the validation period,
  independent from day to day, with a step change in the mean on day 61; @eq-m45-cusum with target 0.
  Random numbers come from a fixed seed, so the picture is repeatable; the recursion is tested
  against `epml.evidence`.
- Shift size, $k$ and $h$ are illustrative, not recommended settings.
- What would change the result: gradual rather than step drift, weekly patterns in case mix,
  correlated days, and a change that alters the labels but not the scores, which a score monitor
  cannot see.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Monitor what you have every day (scores, input statistics), and audit labels on a sample.
- Choose $k$ and $h$ from the false-alarm rate you can afford and the delay you can accept.

### Change control

AI models are updated: retrained on new data, given a new threshold, or given new inputs. For
AI-enabled device software, a predetermined change control plan (PCCP), authorized with the marketing
submission, lets the manufacturer make the planned changes without a new submission for each one
[@fdapccp2024]. The engineering habit behind it is general: **write down the kinds of change you plan
and the acceptance criteria before you see the results**, judge each candidate on a locked test set, and
treat a change the plan did not describe as needing its own review. In lab part E, neither retraining
nor re-tuning the threshold met all the pre-specified criteria after a population shift; a new input
did, but it was outside the plan.

**Key takeaways**

- Acceptance criteria are written before the update, on interval bounds, including subgroups.
- The locked test set must come from the population the model will meet.
- A change outside the plan is a new review, however good its numbers.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where AI in EP stands on the ladder.** For AF recurrence after ablation, a meta-analysis pooled 11
studies of machine-learning and traditional models [@koh2026], and new multicentre models continue to
appear with internal and external validation [@wang2026]; these are rungs 0 and 1. Prospective,
non-randomized work exists for AI-ECG screening [@noseworthy2022]. Randomized trials exist for AI-ECG
detection of low ejection fraction [@yao2021], for AI-guided screening for cardiomyopathy in pregnancy
[@adedinsewo2024], and for AI-guided ablation in persistent AF [@deisenhofer2025]. The 2025 scientific
statement on AI in clinical EP reviewed reporting across AF management, sudden cardiac death and EP-lab
applications and found important items under-reported [@svennberg2025].

**What a randomized trial adds.** It tests the whole intervention, including how clinicians act on the
model's output, against usual care, with outcomes that matter to patients. A retrospective AUC answers
a narrower question: whether the model ranks patients well in data like its own.

**What a reader should ask of an EP AI study:**

- **Which rung?** And which checklist was it reported against?
- **Which population, device and reference standard?** Does the intended population match?
- **What happened after deployment?** Monitoring plan, drift alarms, and the plan for updates.

## How experts think

Before trusting an AI-in-EP result, ask:

1. **Which rung of the ladder?** Internal, external, prospective or randomized; and against which
   checklist [@collins2024; @svennberg2025].
2. **Was the study large enough?** For the interval it reports, given the prevalence (@eq-m45-n-sens).
3. **Does it help a decision?** Net benefit over the relevant thresholds (@eq-m45-net-benefit), and
   calibration (m35).
4. **What happens after deployment?** Monitoring, alarms (@eq-m45-cusum) and audits.
5. **How will it change?** A plan with acceptance criteria fixed in advance [@fdapccp2024].

One sentence to keep: **evidence is a ladder, deployment is a process, and every update is a test
whose pass mark is set before the result is known.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Patients for a sensitivity (@eq-m45-n-sens) | $n = z^2 Se(1-Se)/(d^2\pi)$; for specificity divide by $1-\pi$ |
| Net benefit (@eq-m45-net-benefit) | $\mathrm{TP}/n - (\mathrm{FP}/n)\,p_t/(1-p_t)$; treat all $= \pi - (1-\pi)p_t/(1-p_t)$ |
| CUSUM (@eq-m45-cusum) | $S_t = \max(0, S_{t-1} + x_t - \mu_0 - k)$; alarm at $S_t > h$; delay $\approx h/(\delta - k)$ for large shifts |

**Tools in this module**

| Tool | For | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TRIPOD+AI | Reporting prediction-model studies | @collins2024 |
| PROBAST+AI | Quality, risk of bias and applicability | @moons2025 |
| DECIDE-AI | Early clinical evaluation | @vasey2022 |
| SPIRIT-AI, CONSORT-AI | Trial protocols and reports | @cruzrivera2020, @liu2020 |
| EHRA AI checklist | Reporting AI research in EP | @svennberg2025 |
| PCCP | Planned changes to AI-enabled device software | @fdapccp2024 |

**Rules of thumb**

- Report intervals, calibration and net benefit, not only AUC.
- Monitor scores daily and labels on a sample; set alarm thresholds from the false-alarm rate.
- Fix acceptance criteria before any update, on interval bounds and in subgroups.

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. A paper reports AUC 0.95 for an AF-recurrence model. What do you ask?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Which rung: internal or external validation, and in which centres. Sample size and number of events,
calibration, and net benefit at decision thresholds. How the outcome was ascertained (monitoring
intensity changes recurrence rates). Whether the predictors are available at the time of the
decision. Then appraise it with PROBAST+AI [@moons2025] and check reporting against TRIPOD+AI and the
EHRA checklist [@collins2024; @svennberg2025].

</details>

**Q2. How many patients does a study need to estimate a sensitivity of about 0.9 within ±0.05 if 20% have
the condition?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$1.96^2 \times 0.9 \times 0.1 / (0.05^2 \times 0.2) \approx 692$ (@eq-m45-n-sens) [@buderer1996], of whom
about 138 have the condition. Check the specificity requirement too and enrol the larger number;
inflate for several recordings per patient.

</details>

**Q3. What does a decision curve show that an ROC curve does not?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Whether acting on the model is better than acting on everyone or no one, at the threshold
probabilities clinicians would actually use, with false positives weighted by the odds of the
threshold (@eq-m45-net-benefit) [@vickers2006]. An ROC curve shows ranking only, with no costs and no
prevalence.

</details>

**Q4. How would you monitor a deployed AI-ECG detector when labels arrive months later?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Daily statistics that need no labels, such as the mean score, the share of positives, and input
quality and distributions, each standardized against the validation period and watched with a
CUSUM (@eq-m45-cusum) [@page1954]. Pair it with audits of a labelled sample, and with subgroup checks. Lab part
D shows a drift that left sensitivity almost unchanged while specificity fell, mostly in one subgroup.

</details>

**Q5. How do $k$ and $h$ change a CUSUM?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$k$ is the allowance: deviations smaller than $k$ do not accumulate, so it sets the size of shift the
chart is tuned to. $h$ is the threshold: larger $h$ means rarer false alarms and longer delays. For a
large shift $\delta$ the delay is about $h/(\delta - k)$.

</details>

**Q6. What is a predetermined change control plan, and what goes in one?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

For AI-enabled device software, a plan authorized with the marketing submission that lets the
manufacturer make the planned changes without a new submission for each [@fdapccp2024]. The engineering
content: which changes are planned (for example retraining on new data with the same inputs), how each
will be validated, the acceptance criteria fixed in advance, and how the update is rolled out and
monitored. Lab part E applies the idea; it is not a regulatory template.

</details>

**Q7. A retrained model fixes a subgroup but lowers overall sensitivity. Ship it?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Only if it meets the criteria written before the update, on interval bounds, including the
sensitivity bound. In lab part E neither the retrained model nor its re-tuned threshold passed; the
fix that worked added an input, a change outside the plan that needs its own review.

</details>

**Q8. Why might a model with excellent retrospective AUC fail a randomized trial?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The trial tests the whole intervention: whether clinicians see, trust and act on the output, whether
acting changes outcomes, and whether the trial population resembles the development data. A
retrospective AUC tests none of these. EP has trials that met their endpoints
[@yao2021; @deisenhofer2025], and each reports its effect for its own population and setting.

</details>

**Q9. What did the EHRA AI checklist find about AI-in-EP reporting?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Applied to 55 studies in AF management, sudden cardiac death and EP-lab applications, no item was
reported by more than 55% of papers in any domain, and trial registration, participant details, data
handling and training performance were reported by fewer than 20% [@svennberg2025].

</details>

**Q10. How can several hospitals validate a model without pooling patient data?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Federated learning and evaluation: each site trains or evaluates locally and shares only model updates
or summary results. A federated model across 20 institutes generalized better than single-site models
[@dayan2021]; NVIDIA FLARE is an open framework for this [@roth2022nvflare]. Governance, site
differences and the reference standard still have to be checked site by site.

</details>

**Q11. A drift alarm fires. What next?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Find out what changed before acting: check input data quality and case mix, label a sample, and compare
subgroups. Decide whether the model is still within its validated use; if not, restrict or pause it
and follow the change plan. Record the alarm, the findings and the decision.

</details>

**Q12. Which checklist goes with which study?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

TRIPOD+AI for reporting prediction-model development and validation, PROBAST+AI for appraising them
[@collins2024; @moons2025]; DECIDE-AI for early clinical evaluation [@vasey2022]; SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI
for trial protocols and reports [@cruzrivera2020; @liu2020]; and the EHRA AI checklist for EP studies
[@svennberg2025].

</details>

## Code lab

The Part VII capstone takes the RR-interval AF detector of m37 through a model's life: sample size,
report card, decision curve, deployment, drift and a controlled update.

| Part | What you do | Data |
| --- | --- | --- |

| B | How many patients? (@eq-m45-n-sens), checked by simulation | simulation |

| D | Silent drift and a CUSUM alarm without labels (@eq-m45-cusum) | synthetic ECGs |
| E | Change control: three candidate updates against pre-specified criteria | synthetic ECGs |
| F | Train on one database, monitor on another | Challenge 2017 and PTB-XL (download) |

  (Open Data Commons Attribution v1.0) and PTB-XL 1.0.3 [@wagner2020] (Creative Commons Attribution
  4.0), checked against their published SHA-256 lists; skipped without internet access.
- The change-control part illustrates acceptance criteria fixed in advance; its criteria are ours and
  are not a regulatory template.

Each part ends with **checks**: lines that pass with the code as given. If you change something
and a check fails, that is information, not an error to hide.

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. A condition becomes four times rarer in the study population. What happens to the patients needed
for a given sensitivity interval?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

Four times as many (@eq-m45-n-sens): the denominator holds the prevalence.

</details>

**S2. At a threshold probability of 0.2, what is the net benefit of acting on everyone when prevalence is
0.2?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$0.2 - 0.8 \times 0.25 = 0$ (@eq-m45-net-benefit): at a threshold equal to the prevalence, acting on
everyone is no better than acting on no one.

</details>

**S3. $k = 0.5$, $h = 2$. The standardized daily values are 1.5, 1.5, 1.0. On which day does the CUSUM
alarm?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$S$ = 1.0, 2.0, 2.5 (@eq-m45-cusum): the alarm is on day 3, when $S$ first exceeds 2.

</details>

**S4. Which design can show that using a model improves outcomes?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

A randomized trial comparing care with and without the model, reported with CONSORT-AI [@liu2020].

</details>

**S5. True or false: if a retrained model's AUC is higher, the update can be deployed under the plan.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

False. It must meet every pre-specified criterion, including sensitivity, specificity and subgroups,
and be a kind of change the plan describes.

</details>

**S6. Which tool assesses risk of bias in a prediction-model study?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

PROBAST+AI [@moons2025].

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Decision curves.** Vickers and Elkin introduced the decision curve with a worked example in
  prostate cancer; look at how the model's curve compares with "treat all" and "treat none" across
  thresholds [@vickers2006; [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2577036/)].
  Compare with @eq-m45-net-benefit and lab part C.
- **The PROBAST+AI structure.** Moons and colleagues set out the two parts (development and
  evaluation) and four domains of the tool [@moons2025;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11931409/)]. This module: the evidence ladder.

## Further reading

- **Reporting and appraisal.** @collins2024, @moons2025, @vasey2022, @cruzrivera2020, @liu2020, and for
